The advantage increases with the size of the entangled state, however generating and preserving large entangled states remains a major experimental challenge. Multipass protocols offer an alternative approach by allowing a single probe to interact repeatedly with the parameter of interest, but their performance is highly susceptible to loss, which accumulates over successive passes and rapidly erodes the quantum advantage. Here we introduce a hybrid strategy that combines small, loss-resilient entangled states with multipass interferometry. We show that this approach retains the robustness of small entangled probes while exploiting repeated interactions to achieve substantial enhancements in measurement precision. Furthermore, we propose a concrete implementation using currently available technologies, demonstrating that the predicted performance gains should be experimentally accessible with existing capabilities.
one_liner: Small loss-resilient entangled probes combined with multipass interferometry can boost precision without requiring large fragile entangled states.
why_it_matters: It targets a practical route to quantum-enhanced sensing under realistic optical loss using experimentally available components.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid metrology protocol where a small entangled state interrogates a parameter through multiple passes. This keeps the robustness of modest entanglement while accumulating phase information through repeated interactions. The authors present a concrete implementation path and argue the predicted gains are accessible with current technology.
main_result: A hybrid small-entangled-state multipass scheme is predicted to retain quantum precision gains in lossy interferometric sensing.
application_angle: The approach is relevant to deployable precision interferometers where optical loss makes large entangled probes impractical.

title: Light-Hole Spin Qubits in Strained SiGe Lattice-Matched to Ge
abstract: Strained germanium ($\varepsilon$-Ge) quantum wells on metamorphic SiGe buffers have enabled advanced hole-based spin qubit devices. Alternatively, unstrained Ge with lattice-matched strained silicon-germanium ($\varepsilon$-SiGe) barriers eliminates the need for metamorphic buffers altogether. The ground state character of both these platforms is predominantly heavy-hole (HH) with a largely anisotropic spin response. We propose and study an alternative heterostructure, lattice-matched to Ge, in which both the SiGe quantum well and barriers are tensile strained, with their composition contrast providing the band offset for confinement and the tensile strain stabilizing a light-hole (LH) ground state. We show large spin-orbit coupling (SOC), both linear and cubic, along with a significantly more isotropic spin response compared to strained HH qubits. We also study the decoherence properties of the proposed device, showing an appreciable gain in the quality factor compared to their HH counterparts. Finally, we propose a bilayer heterostructure that allows for electrical switching between HH and LH ground state character.
one_liner: A tensile-strained SiGe/Ge-compatible heterostructure is proposed to realize light-hole spin qubits with strong SOC and improved isotropy.
why_it_matters: It offers a materials-level route to hole-spin qubits with better control properties and quality factors than heavy-hole designs.
detailed_summary: The authors study a Ge-lattice-matched SiGe heterostructure where tensile strain in both well and barriers stabilizes a light-hole ground state. Calculations indicate large linear and cubic spin-orbit coupling and a more isotropic spin response compared with strained heavy-hole qubits. They also analyze decoherence and propose a bilayer design enabling electrical switching between heavy-hole and light-hole ground-state character.
main_result: The proposed lattice-matched tensile SiGe design yields a light-hole qubit with strong SOC, improved spin isotropy, and higher estimated quality factor.
application_angle: This could improve electrically controlled semiconductor qubits while simplifying epitaxy by avoiding metamorphic buffer requirements.

title: Surpassing Gaussian optimality in multiparameter estimation with indefinite causal order
abstract: We identify single-mode Gaussian probes, generated by displacement and squeezing operations on the vacuum state, which are optimal for the simultaneous estimation of displacement and squeezing operations in continuous-variable quantum systems. Importantly, our results reveal that the best precision at a fixed energy is achieved not by an experimentally costly squeezing resource, but rather by redirecting some of the energy towards displacement, thus allowing for more resource-effective operations. Furthermore, introducing indefinite causal order (ICO) in either the probe preparation or parameter encoding step can surpass the Gaussian precision bound, even though the optimal Gaussian probe state is agnostic to the ordering of the operations. Specifically, we observe that odd-parity superpositions of the two definite orders can enhance precision over optimal Gaussian probes in specific parameter regimes. Further, the observed advantage cannot be attributed solely to non-Gaussianity, as quantified by the relative entropy of non-Gaussianity, highlighting ICO as an independent resource for enhancing multiparameter estimation.
one_liner: Indefinite causal order can exceed the best single-mode Gaussian precision bound for continuous-variable multiparameter estimation.
why_it_matters: It identifies ICO as a distinct metrological resource beyond Gaussian squeezing or generic non-Gaussianity.
detailed_summary: The paper determines optimal single-mode Gaussian probes for simultaneous estimation of displacement and squeezing operations at fixed energy. It finds that allocating energy to displacement, not only squeezing, can be optimal within the Gaussian class. Introducing indefinite causal order in preparation or encoding, especially through odd-parity superpositions of operation orders, surpasses the Gaussian bound in selected regimes.
main_result: Odd-parity superpositions of definite operation orders are shown to improve estimation precision beyond optimal Gaussian probes in some parameter regimes.
application_angle: The result points to new resource engineering strategies for precision optical sensing and continuous-variable quantum technologies.

title: Room-temperature graphene sub-terahertz detector integrated on a silicon dielectric waveguide
abstract: Terahertz (THz) photonics offers a promising platform for next-generation 6G wireless communications, on-chip spectrometers, and non-invasive biomedical sensors. In the near- and mid-infrared, monolithically integrated photodetectors are a cornerstone of photonic integrated circuits (PICs). In the THz range, however, such integration on low-loss dielectric waveguides remains an open challenge: to date, room-temperature on-waveguide detection has been realized only through hybrid flip-chip assembly of discrete elements, which leads to poor mode coupling, larger footprint, and reduced mechanical stability. Here we address this gap by demonstrating a room-temperature graphene sub-THz detector monolithically integrated on a high-resistivity silicon dielectric waveguide for D-band (110-170 GHz) operation. We couple an hBN-encapsulated graphene channel to the guided mode using a tapered slot-line antenna patterned directly onto the silicon surface. The detector achieves a voltage responsivity of 11.5 V/W and a 3 dB bandwidth of 1.94 GHz, with the latter currently limited by parasitic inductance of the readout interconnects rather than by the intrinsic graphene response. This platform provides a practical pathway to fully integrated room-temperature THz photonic circuits, where electrostatic gating and impedance matching can improve both responsivity and bandwidth by roughly an order of magnitude.
one_liner: A monolithic graphene detector on a high-resistivity silicon waveguide enables room-temperature D-band sub-THz photonic detection.
why_it_matters: It addresses a key integration gap for compact THz photonic circuits by avoiding flip-chip detector assembly.
detailed_summary: The authors demonstrate an hBN-encapsulated graphene channel coupled to a guided D-band mode through a tapered slot-line antenna patterned on silicon. The room-temperature on-waveguide detector reaches 11.5 V/W voltage responsivity and 1.94 GHz 3 dB bandwidth. The bandwidth is attributed to parasitic readout inductance rather than graphene’s intrinsic speed, suggesting room for improved impedance-matched designs.
main_result: The device demonstrates monolithic room-temperature D-band detection on a silicon dielectric waveguide with 11.5 V/W responsivity and 1.94 GHz bandwidth.
application_angle: The platform supports integrated THz links, spectrometers, and sensor circuits for 6G, biomedical, and on-chip photonics applications.

title: Distributed Trotterization with optimal time-scaling entanglement cost
abstract: Distributed architectures extend quantum simulation of many-body dynamics beyond the reach of any single processor, with shared entanglement mediating interactions between spatially separated devices. Conventional implementations rely on quantum teleportation, which provides a universal realization of nonlocal operations but incurs a fixed entanglement cost per gate, irrespective of its strength. This becomes increasingly inefficient in product formula simulation, where higher accuracy requires ever more numerous, yet progressively weaker, nonlocal rotations, causing the entanglement cost to diverge in the high-accuracy limit. Here we introduce a simple repeat-until-success protocol that makes entanglement consumption adaptive to interaction strength. Incorporating this primitive into distributed product formulas yields a total entanglement cost that scales linearly with evolution time and remains independent of Trotter error. A matching lower bound from quantum communication complexity proves this time scaling to be optimal, establishing a resource-efficient foundation for high-accuracy quantum simulation across networked processors.
one_liner: A repeat-until-success primitive reduces entanglement use for distributed Trotter simulation to optimal linear-in-time scaling.
why_it_matters: It targets a concrete bottleneck in networked quantum processors: nonlocal simulation gates no longer require entanglement cost that diverges with accuracy.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a repeat-until-success implementation for weak nonlocal rotations whose average entanglement consumption adapts to the rotation strength. When inserted into product-formula simulation, this removes the usual divergence of teleportation-based entanglement cost as Trotter steps become finer. A communication-complexity lower bound shows the resulting linear scaling with evolution time is optimal.
main_result: Distributed product-formula simulation can achieve entanglement cost linear in simulated evolution time and independent of Trotter error.
application_angle: This makes high-accuracy quantum simulation across modular processors more resource-efficient and better matched to limited interconnect entanglement rates.

title: Structured Non-Locality and Emergent Locality in Cavity-QED Many-Body Dynamics
abstract: Cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED) modifies many-body systems by combining cavity-mediated collective interactions with microscopic short-range interactions. The resulting dynamics lies between the local and fully collective limits, such that neither locality nor collectivity alone provides a complete organizing principle. In the clean conceptual limit of dominant collective coupling, we show that the effective dynamics within each energetically isolated subspace is generically controlled by whether that subspace admits a local product-state basis, and identify exceptions imposed by angular-momentum selection rules. Product-state subspaces generically retain the spatial structure of the microscopic interaction. Entangled subspaces instead generically dress local processes with global operators, generating non-local but highly structured dynamics. We illustrate this by deriving the corresponding effective Hamiltonians in two representative cavity-QED spin models. The cavity-isolated subspace thus becomes a resource for generating competing short-range interactions or globally conditioned local processes, opening a class of many-body dynamics without local or fully collective counterparts.
one_liner: Cavity-isolated many-body subspaces can preserve locality or generate structured nonlocal dynamics depending on their state structure.
why_it_matters: It clarifies how cavity QED can engineer dynamics beyond purely local or fully collective models, useful for analog quantum simulation design.
detailed_summary: The work analyzes many-body cavity-QED systems in the limit where collective cavity coupling energetically isolates subspaces. It shows that product-state subspaces tend to retain the microscopic short-range interaction structure, while entangled subspaces dress local processes with global operators. Two representative cavity-QED spin models are used to derive effective Hamiltonians illustrating these structured nonlocal processes.
main_result: The authors identify when cavity-isolated subspaces yield emergent local interactions versus globally conditioned local dynamics.
application_angle: The framework helps design cavity-mediated quantum simulators with tunable competition between short-range physics and structured nonlocal control.

title: Switchable heavy-hole/light-hole spin qubit
abstract: Compressively strained Ge quantum wells in planar SiGe/Ge heterostructures are the state-of-the-art platform for hole spin qubits. While they exhibit robust coherence times, they possess weak intrinsic spin-orbit interaction (SOI) due to the heavy-hole (HH) character of the wavefunction. Recently, light-hole (LH) qubits were proposed in GeSn/Ge heterostructures, offering strong, intrinsic, linear-in-momentum SOI. In this work, we propose a switchable HH-LH spin qubit in a bilayer Ge heterostructure with SiGeSn barriers, combining the advantages of HH and LH devices. The character of the qubit can be changed by shuttling from an LH well to an HH well, which also enables fast, hopping-based single-qubit rotations. Additionally, we observe an HH-LH resonance introduced by the in-plane confinement, resulting in $g$-factor peaks and first-order charge noise sweet spots. Our calculations reveal a sweet spot with Rabi frequencies on the order of 100 MHz, comparable to the LH regime, but with a more than tenfold increase in coherence time, on the order of 100 $μ$s.
one_liner: A bilayer Ge design switches between heavy-hole and light-hole spin-qubit regimes to combine coherence and fast control.
why_it_matters: It proposes a semiconductor qubit architecture that addresses the usual tradeoff between long coherence and strong spin-orbit-driven manipulation.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a SiGeSn-barrier bilayer Ge heterostructure in which a hole qubit can be shuttled between light-hole and heavy-hole wells. The light-hole character gives strong intrinsic spin-orbit interaction for fast control, while the heavy-hole character supports improved coherence. Calculations identify an in-plane-confinement-induced HH-LH resonance with g-factor peaks and first-order charge-noise sweet spots.
main_result: The design predicts about 100 MHz Rabi frequencies together with coherence times near 100 microseconds at a charge-noise sweet spot.
application_angle: Such switchable operation could improve gate speed and fidelity in scalable planar semiconductor quantum processors.

title: Computing key rates for one-sided device-independent quantum key distribution
abstract: The defining feature of one-sided device-independent quantum key distribution is its asymmetric trust model in which only one party is characterized. This scenario sets an interesting middle ground between high key rates achievable by characterizing devices and the security of full device-independence. Here, we provide new tools, methods, and benchmarks for calculating key rates in this setting. To achieve this, we develop and compare two extensions of the NPA hierarchy and derive finite-size security bounds against general attacks with arbitrary device memory. The latter is based on the Generalized Entropy Accumulation Theorem. We then investigate the performance of various protocols: the BB84 protocol both with and without losses, a qutrit mutually unbiased bases protocol, and protocols based on Bell inequalties such as CHSH and $I_{3322}$. We find that the choice of which party is characterized can strongly affects the key rate, surprisingly without a universal ordering. Our work thus offers a general toolbox for calculating key rates for one-sided device-independent QKD protocols.
one_liner: New semidefinite and finite-size tools benchmark key rates for one-sided device-independent QKD protocols.
why_it_matters: It gives practitioners methods to quantify secure key generation in the middle ground between trusted-device and fully device-independent QKD.
detailed_summary: The paper develops two extensions of the NPA hierarchy for computing key rates in one-sided device-independent QKD. It also derives finite-size security bounds against general attacks with arbitrary device memory using the Generalized Entropy Accumulation Theorem. Benchmarks cover BB84 with and without loss, qutrit mutually unbiased bases protocols, and Bell-inequality-based schemes such as CHSH and I3322.
main_result: The authors provide a general computational toolbox and show that which party is characterized can strongly affect the achievable key rate.
application_angle: The results support more realistic security-performance evaluation for QKD systems where only one device side can be fully trusted.

title: Entirely nonlocal quantum magic without entanglement
abstract: Nonstabilizerness, or magic, is an archetypal \emph{quantum} resource that is necessary for quantum computational advantage. Here we uncover a phenomenon seemingly at odds with the quantum nature of magic: entirely nonlocal magic (ENM)---magic present only in correlations and absent from each party's marginal---can live without entanglement. We systematically study this separation and show it is universal and operationally reversible: every magical state or channel can be encoded into and recovered from a separable ENM realization using only local stabilizer processing and classical communication. We leverage this mechanism to devise an activation key protocol in which a classical key controls access to non-Clifford operations. We further formulate magic secret sharing, in which computational power inaccessible to any party alone becomes accessible through cooperation. On a superconducting quantum processor, we experimentally demonstrate activation key and network computing primitives, together with separable ENM state preparation and extraction protocols. Together, our results establish that magic can be classically activated, localized, and secret-shared without entanglement, providing new resource-control primitives for distributed quantum computation.
one_liner: Magic can be stored entirely in separable correlations and activated without entanglement on a superconducting processor.
why_it_matters: It separates nonstabilizerness from entanglement operationally, opening new control primitives for distributed quantum computation.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces entirely nonlocal magic, where nonstabilizerness exists only in correlations while local marginals remain nonmagical. It proves that every magical state or channel can be encoded into and recovered from a separable realization using local stabilizer processing and classical communication. Experiments on a superconducting quantum processor demonstrate activation-key and network-computing primitives, plus state preparation and extraction protocols.
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrate separable entirely nonlocal magic and its use for classically controlled access to non-Clifford resources.
application_angle: This suggests ways to gate, share, and activate computational power in distributed quantum workflows without relying on entanglement distribution.

title: Dissipatively Stabilized 0-n Fock Qubits for Noise-Biased Quantum Computing
abstract: Noise-biased qubits have bit-flip errors that are exponentially suppressed relative to phase-flip errors, and offer a promising route toward fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, this bias can be compromised during gate operations with non-biased control qubits. To address this limitation, we propose a "0-n" Fock qubit architecture that maintains the noise bias by encoding information in the ground state and n-th excited state of a nonlinear multi-level system, such as a transmon. This encoding is achieved via a dissipative stabilization that acts as decay and gain for lower and upper intermediate levels, respectively. We first analytically demonstrate that bit-flip errors are exponentially suppressed with the number of levels. Then, we present a practical implementation using a multi-mode lossy filter to achieve the frequency-selective dissipation. Finally, we numerically demonstrate that bit-flip probabilities approaching $10^{-8}$ are achievable for controlled-X gates on cat qubits using the 0-n qubit as an ancilla with $n \geq 9$ (i.e. ten or more levels), for realistic experimental parameters. Building on this, we simulate syndrome extraction in a repetition code, achieving logical error rates in the megaquop regime with only a distance of $d=9$.
one_liner: A dissipatively stabilized 0-n Fock qubit preserves noise bias for cat-qubit gates and syndrome extraction.
why_it_matters: It proposes a hardware-level route to keep exponentially suppressed bit flips even when biased qubits interact with ancilla controls.
detailed_summary: The work encodes a qubit in the ground and n-th excited states of a nonlinear multilevel system and stabilizes it through engineered dissipation on intermediate levels. Analytic arguments show bit-flip errors are exponentially suppressed with the number of levels, and a lossy multimode filter is proposed for frequency-selective dissipation. Numerical simulations show controlled-X gates on cat qubits with 0-n ancillas can reach bit-flip probabilities near 1e-8 for n at least 9 under realistic parameters.
main_result: The architecture maintains strong noise bias during ancilla-mediated cat-qubit operations and enables megaquop-regime repetition-code simulations at distance 9.
application_angle: It could reduce overhead for fault-tolerant architectures that rely on biased-noise qubits and repeated syndrome extraction.

title: The Gain-Engineered Transmon
abstract: The interaction between a qubit and its environment can be engineered such that one error channel dominates over all others, resulting in noise bias. This property enables error correction codes to focus on the dominant error type, thereby significantly reducing the number of physical systems required for fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, engineering noise bias typically introduces complexity at the physical system level, which decreases its usefulness by limiting scalability. Here, we introduce and experimentally realize a noise-biased qubit in a standard transmon-readout resonator circuit, one of the most common superconducting architectures, by only adding a single microwave tone. We encode the qubit in the transmon $|\mathrm{g}\rangle$- and $|\mathrm{f}\rangle$-states, and engineer a frequency-selective gain channel that counteracts single-photon loss errors between the computational states. We demonstrate an order-of-magnitude enhancement in relaxation time compared to the $|\mathrm{g}\rangle-|\mathrm{e}\rangle$ encoding, conceding only a factor-of-two decrease in the echo-coherence time. Furthermore, we show that this qubit is compatible with fast, high-fidelity operations. Our results open a path towards using this system as a simple building-block for hardware-efficient quantum error detection and correction schemes.
one_liner: A standard transmon circuit is turned into a noise-biased g-f qubit using only a single microwave gain tone.
why_it_matters: It offers a low-overhead route to biased-noise superconducting qubits without exotic circuit redesign, relevant to hardware-efficient error correction.
detailed_summary: The work encodes a qubit in the ground and second-excited states of a transmon and adds a frequency-selective gain channel to counteract single-photon loss between computational states. Experimentally, the authors report an order-of-magnitude relaxation-time improvement over the usual g-e encoding, with about a factor-of-two echo-coherence penalty. They also show compatibility with fast, high-fidelity operations in a standard transmon-readout resonator architecture.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates a microwave-tone-enabled noise-biased transmon qubit with much longer relaxation time and usable fast gates.
application_angle: The approach could simplify biased-noise building blocks for quantum error detection and correction in scalable superconducting processors.

title: Immittance formulas for exact blackbox quantization and divergence-free effective models in circuit QED
abstract: Building on the first-order circuit quantization method [arXiv:2304.12252, arXiv:2401.09120], we provide simple formulas to construct exact Hamiltonians for Josephson-junction-based superconducting qudits capacitively, inductively, or galvanically coupled to passive linear environments. These environments may be multiport, multimode, discrete or continuous, reciprocal or nonreciprocal, and are characterized directly by their impedance or admittance matrices. In the weak-coupling regime, we further derive \emph{divergence-free} dispersive Hamiltonians for mode-resolved environments and transition-resolved weak-coupling master equations for dissipative continua. Mode structure, frequency renormalizations, environment-mediated interactions, decay rates, and directional cross couplings then follow from the same causal immittance response, while spurious Lamb-shift divergences arising from uncontrolled approximations in previous treatments are made explicit and avoided. We apply the theory to a set of illustrative circuits comprising a discrete resonator filter, finite-band metamaterial environments, nonreciprocal waveguide-QED systems, and superconducting giant atoms, for which analytical response matrices can be obtained, although the method is particularly well suited to numerical responses from electromagnetic solvers or experimental characterization. We thereby extend the black-box quantization framework to multiport, dissipative, and nonreciprocal settings, establishing a simple and scalable route toward optimized and automated electromagnetic design of large-scale superconducting quantum hardware.
one_liner: The paper gives exact immittance-based Hamiltonian formulas for blackbox quantization of complex circuit-QED environments.
why_it_matters: It makes automated electromagnetic design of superconducting quantum hardware more reliable by avoiding spurious divergences in effective models.
detailed_summary: The authors extend first-order circuit quantization to Josephson-junction qudits coupled capacitively, inductively, or galvanically to passive linear environments described by impedance or admittance matrices. In weak coupling, they derive divergence-free dispersive Hamiltonians and master equations that consistently yield renormalizations, decay rates, interactions, and directional couplings. The framework covers multiport, multimode, dissipative, continuous, and nonreciprocal settings, including resonator filters, metamaterials, waveguide QED, and giant atoms.
main_result: The main result is a scalable exact-quantization and effective-model recipe based directly on causal immittance responses.
application_angle: It supports design automation for large superconducting quantum chips using simulated or experimentally measured electromagnetic response matrices.

title: A heterogeneously integrated coupled-cavity frequency beam splitter
abstract: Frequency encoded photonic qubits promise a scalable path towards high-dimensional quantum information processing, but require efficient components for coherently mixing frequency modes. Coupled cavity modulators provide this functionality by using only a single driving microwave tone to couple hybridized optical supermodes. Here, we demonstrate a heterogeneously integrated thin-film lithium-niobate-on-silicon coupled-cavity modulator that realizes tunable bidirectional frequency mode transformations, including \(50/50\) beam splitting and near complete frequency swapping with \(>20~\mathrm{dB}\) pump extinction at a \(10~\mathrm{GHz}\) supermode splitting. Because the electro-optic film is bonded onto a foundry fabricated silicon photonics platform, the approach is compatible with co-integration of photon pair sources, spectral filters, active tuning elements, and single photon detectors. We also bond thin-film lithium tantalate onto the same coupled-cavity platform, demonstrating material flexibility for scalable integrated frequency bin quantum photonic circuits.
one_liner: A bonded thin-film lithium-niobate-on-silicon coupled-cavity modulator acts as a tunable frequency-bin beam splitter.
why_it_matters: Efficient coherent mixing of frequency modes is a key missing primitive for scalable frequency-encoded integrated quantum photonics.
detailed_summary: The device uses coupled optical cavities and a single microwave tone to couple hybridized optical supermodes separated by 10 GHz. The authors demonstrate bidirectional frequency transformations, including 50/50 splitting and near-complete frequency swapping, with greater than 20 dB pump extinction. The heterogeneous platform is also shown with lithium tantalate, indicating material flexibility on a foundry silicon photonics base.
main_result: The experiment realizes tunable frequency-bin beam splitting and swapping in a heterogeneously integrated photonic circuit.
application_angle: The component is compatible with co-integrated sources, filters, tuners, and detectors for frequency-bin quantum processors and communication links.

title: Depth Control of Room-Temperature Quantum Emitters in Gallium Nitride
abstract: Bright quantum emitters are key components for quantum communication systems. Radiative point defects in gallium nitride (GaN) are promising candidates for room-temperature single-photon emission, operating from the visible to the telecom O-band. Despite their potential, their integration into photonic structures has remained limited in the literature, with experimental photon extraction efficiencies far below simulated predictions. To identify the origin of this limitation, we investigate visible and near-infrared quantum emitters in GaN epilayers grown on $c$-plane sapphire substrates exhibiting narrow linewidths ($\sim$4 nm), high photon count rates ($ > $2 MHz), and strong antibunching, reaching $g^{(2)}(0)$ values as low as 0.06 at room temperature. We find that these emitters are located near the GaN/substrate interface, explaining their limited coupling to optical modes. Building on this observation, we show that the insertion of a thin low-temperature GaN interlayer enables the formation of quantum emitters at arbitrary depths with sub-60 nm accuracy, independent of the substrate. The intentionally introduced emitters retain optical properties comparable to naturally occurring ones, including narrow linewidths ($\sim$6 nm), saturation count rates exceeding 1.5 MHz, high Debye-Waller factors (0.69-0.98), and strong antibunching. The resulting epilayer fully coalesces within less than 250 nm ensuring compatibility with GaN-based cavity fabrication and enabling emitter placement within intrinsic regions of p-i-n diode architectures. These results mark a decisive step toward efficient emitter-cavity coupling, enabling the realization of cavity-enhanced quantum emission in GaN.
one_liner: GaN quantum emitters are depth-controlled with sub-60 nm accuracy while retaining bright room-temperature single-photon emission.
why_it_matters: Controlled emitter placement addresses a practical bottleneck in coupling GaN defects to cavities and diode-integrated photonic structures.
detailed_summary: The study finds that naturally occurring visible and near-infrared GaN emitters lie near the GaN/substrate interface, explaining poor extraction relative to simulations. By inserting a thin low-temperature GaN interlayer, the authors intentionally form emitters at arbitrary depths with sub-60 nm accuracy. The created emitters preserve strong antibunching, narrow linewidths, MHz-class saturation count rates, and high Debye-Waller factors while remaining compatible with coalesced GaN epilayers and p-i-n structures.
main_result: The work demonstrates deterministic depth placement of bright GaN single-photon emitters without sacrificing key optical properties.
application_angle: It enables better emitter-cavity alignment for efficient GaN-based quantum light sources in integrated photonics and quantum communication.

title: Parity Anomaly as Modular Commutator with Massless Dirac Fermion
abstract: The modular commutator $J(A,B,C) = i\langle[K_{AB},K_{BC}]\rangle$ extracts the chiral central charge $c_-$ from a single bulk wavefunction of a \emph{gapped} 2d state, where $3J/π=c_-$. Inspired by the recent developments in the field of gapless symmetry-protected topological phases, we ask: what does the modular commutator measure, if it is well-defined at all, when the 2d bulk becomes \textit{gapless}? Several interesting new insights can already be obtained using the simple Haldane honeycomb model. For the critical point hosting an isolated Dirac node we find that $J$ remains sharp: it converges to a \textit{half-quantized} value, with corrections that decay as a power law in the subsystem size rather than exponentially, mirroring the power-law correlations in gapless systems. We prove the half-quantization using an emergent reflection symmetry of the massless Dirac cone, and show that the half-quantized contribution comes from the other gapped cone (the massive partner of the massless one). This massive partner can be interpreted as the physical incarnation of the Pauli-Villars regulator, which is the origin of the parity-breaking level-$\frac{1}{2}$ Chern-Simons term (with half-quantized Hall conductance) and the parity anomaly. When protected chiral edge modes coexist with a bulk Dirac node we obtain $3J/π= c_-+\frac{1}{2}$. The half-quantization is also shown to be robust against tripartition deformation, tuning Dirac velocity and Dirac cone anisotropy. We further investigate other types of gaplessness---quadratic nodes (in contrast to linear Dirac) and the case with Fermi surface---and show that the robust half-quantization of $J$ is lost in such non-Dirac cases. These results generalize the modular commutator beyond gapped phases, and at the same time provide an information-theoretic measurement of the parity anomaly.
one_liner: The modular commutator remains sharp at a massless Dirac critical point and reveals a half-quantized parity-anomaly contribution.
why_it_matters: It proposes an information-theoretic observable for diagnosing parity anomaly physics directly from a bulk wavefunction.
detailed_summary: Using the Haldane honeycomb model, the authors study what the modular commutator measures when a 2D system becomes gapless. At an isolated massless Dirac node, the quantity converges to a half-quantized value with power-law finite-size corrections, unlike the exponential behavior of gapped phases. They connect the effect to the massive partner cone as a physical Pauli-Villars regulator and show robustness to tripartition deformation, velocity tuning, and anisotropy, while non-Dirac gapless cases lose the quantization.
platform_or_system: massless Dirac fermion in the Haldane model
main_result: The main result is half-quantization of the modular commutator at a Dirac critical point, yielding 3J/pi = c_- + 1/2 when chiral edge modes coexist.
application_angle: The method could become a numerical or information-theoretic diagnostic for topological anomaly signatures in quantum many-body platforms.

title: Fast GHZ encoding with $1-o(1)$ fidelity
abstract: We prove that $(1-o(1))$-fidelity $N$-qubit Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) encoding can be performed in time $O(\log N/N)$ using all-to-all 2-local Hamiltonians with bounded 2-qubit interaction terms. This saturates the theoretical lower bound $Ω(\log N/N)$, and by rescaling, also saturates the lower bound on signaling time for Hamiltonians with power-law interaction strengths $1/r^γ$, $γ<d$ in dimension $d$. The protocol uses spin-squeezing dynamics combined with quantum signal processing.
one_liner: A spin-squeezing and quantum-signal-processing protocol reaches near-unit-fidelity GHZ encoding at the optimal all-to-all speed limit.
why_it_matters: Fast GHZ-state preparation is a core primitive for metrology, entanglement generation, and quantum hardware benchmarking.
detailed_summary: The paper proves that N-qubit GHZ encoding with 1-o(1) fidelity can be achieved in O(log N/N) time using all-to-all two-local Hamiltonians with bounded two-qubit terms. This matches the theoretical lower bound and also saturates the corresponding signaling-time bound for sufficiently long-range power-law interactions after rescaling. The protocol combines spin-squeezing dynamics with quantum signal processing rather than relying on sequential gate constructions.
main_result: The main result is an asymptotically optimal near-unit-fidelity GHZ encoding protocol with O(log N/N) runtime.
application_angle: The construction informs how long-range-interaction quantum hardware can prepare macroscopic entanglement rapidly for sensing and computation.

title: Bosonic Encodings for Hermite-Galerkin Discretizations of High-Dimensional PDEs and Bayesian Inverse Problems
abstract: The Koopman-von Neumann framework has been proposed to design quantum algorithms for non-linear dynamics. It maps a non-linear ordinary differential equation to a linear partial differential equation (PDE) governing a probability amplitude. Previous works represents this amplitude in the Hermite-function basis, equivalently as a bosonic state, and truncates the total Hermite degree to obtain a representation over $Θ(m\log N)$ qubits, where $N$ is the number of variables and $m$ the truncation order. We extend this approach to a broader class of linear PDEs whose differential operators have a structured polynomial form. We prove convergence of the truncation for both time-dependent dynamics and gapped ground-state problems under explicit regularity and stability assumptions. We then introduce a qubit encoding that supports efficient block encodings of the truncated operators. Finally, we apply the framework to Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors and observation noise, reducing posterior-state preparation to the preparation of a structured Hamiltonian's ground state.
one_liner: Bosonic Hermite-Galerkin encodings extend KvN-style quantum PDE methods to structured linear PDEs and Bayesian inverse problems.
why_it_matters: It gives a route to quantum algorithms for high-dimensional inverse problems, linking PDE discretization, block encodings, and posterior-state preparation.
detailed_summary: The paper generalizes Hermite-function bosonic representations from nonlinear dynamics to structured linear PDE operators. It proves truncation convergence for time evolution and gapped ground states under explicit regularity and stability assumptions. For Bayesian inverse problems with Gaussian priors and noise, posterior preparation is reduced to preparing the ground state of a structured Hamiltonian.
main_result: The authors provide convergent truncated bosonic PDE encodings with efficient block encodings and an application to Bayesian posterior-state preparation.
application_angle: The framework is relevant to sensing and imaging workflows where high-dimensional inverse problems dominate the computational cost.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum computation cannot be achieved with constant spacetime overhead
abstract: The threshold theorem states that quantum computations can be made reliable below a physical error threshold, at the cost of additional physical qubits and circuit depth. Recent work has reduced these space and time overheads to polylogarithmic or nearly logarithmic scalings, but whether the cumulative spacetime overhead can be constant has remained unclear. Here, we show that even for the simplest task of preserving quantum information in a quantum memory, under an optimistic noise model and allowing general adaptive protocols, there is an unavoidable logarithmic contribution to the cumulative spacetime overhead. This additional cost can nevertheless be shared among many logical qubits, so sufficiently wide computations, including standard implementations of Shor's algorithm, may still achieve constant relative overhead. We further give a positive-rate CSS code construction that attains the memory bound, identify sufficient conditions under which the same scaling extends from quantum memory to fault-tolerant circuit implementations, and derive circuit-size bounds for subsystem spacetime codes. Our work establishes fundamental limits on the resources required for quantum fault tolerance.
one_liner: Fault-tolerant quantum memory and computation require at least logarithmic cumulative spacetime overhead in general.
why_it_matters: It sets a fundamental resource lower bound for scalable quantum hardware, clarifying when constant relative overhead is and is not possible.
detailed_summary: The work proves that even preserving quantum information in memory cannot achieve constant cumulative spacetime overhead under an optimistic noise model with adaptive protocols. The unavoidable extra cost is logarithmic, though it can be amortized across many logical qubits in sufficiently wide computations. The paper also gives a positive-rate CSS construction attaining the memory bound and discusses extensions to fault-tolerant circuits and subsystem spacetime codes.
main_result: The main result is a logarithmic lower bound on cumulative spacetime overhead for reliable quantum information storage.
application_angle: These bounds inform architecture-level resource estimates for practical quantum computers and long-lived quantum communication memories.

title: Enhancing the phase sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer beyond the Heisenberg limit through dynamic squeezing
abstract: We propose a method to enhance the phase sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, independent of its input states. This is achieved by applying squeezing sequences to one arm of the interferometer. By alternating between squeezing along orthogonal quadratures, we demonstrate that the phase sensitivity of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer can be generically enhanced. Since this enhancement is independent of the input states, the proposed dynamic squeezing method allows for further improvement in phase sensitivity when combined with non-classical input states. We compare the dynamic squeezing approach with existing quantum sensing protocols and show that super-Heisenberg scaling can be achieved. Finally, we demonstrate that the scheme is robust against moderate photon loss.
one_liner: Dynamic squeezing in one interferometer arm can enhance Mach-Zehnder phase sensitivity independent of the input state.
why_it_matters: The proposal offers a state-agnostic sensitivity booster that can be combined with nonclassical inputs and remains useful under moderate loss.
detailed_summary: The scheme applies alternating squeezing operations along orthogonal quadratures in one arm of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The authors argue that this generically improves phase sensitivity without relying on a specific input state. They compare the method with existing quantum sensing protocols, report super-Heisenberg scaling, and analyze robustness against moderate photon loss.
main_result: The paper demonstrates a protocol for input-independent phase-sensitivity enhancement using dynamic squeezing sequences.
application_angle: It could improve optical phase metrology in interferometric sensors while remaining compatible with existing nonclassical-state strategies.

title: Recovery-Free CHSH Nonlocality with Particle Loss
abstract: Can CHSH nonlocality survive particle loss without applying an explicit recovery operation? In principle, any deterministic recovery can be absorbed into the measurement. Operationally, we show that the answer depends on the allowed measurements on the lossy system. We distinguish flagged erasure, in which each lost particle leaves a detectable record, from unflagged deletion, in which no such record remains. For flagged erasure and survival probability $η>1/2$, using known quantum-capacity results, we show measurements that asymptotically approach the quantum maximum $2\sqrt2$. In contrast, for $η\le1/2$, CHSH violation is impossible for both loss models. Then, we construct explicit recovery-free protocols using permutation-invariant encodings built from $n$-qubit Dicke states $| D_N^n\rangle$ and measurements on the surviving particles. A one-excitation $(N=1)$ encoding violates CHSH for $η>1/\sqrt{2}$. Increasing the excitation number $N$ yields a family of protocols that violates CHSH for $η>η_G=(\sqrt{5}-1)/2$, with the asymptotic golden ratio approached as $N \to \infty$. Finally, we present a sparse-deletion binomial PI protocol that guarantees CHSH violation for up to $O(\sqrt n)$ deletion errors. Our results distinguish fundamental limits imposed by loss from those set by explicit measurements without recovery.
one_liner: CHSH nonlocality can survive particle loss without explicit recovery when suitable loss-aware measurements and encodings are available.
why_it_matters: It sharpens practical Bell-test and photonic-network limits by separating flagged erasure, unflagged deletion, and measurement constraints.
detailed_summary: The paper studies recovery-free CHSH violation under particle loss and distinguishes flagged erasure from unflagged deletion. It shows violation is impossible for survival probability at or below 1/2, while flagged erasure above 1/2 can asymptotically approach the Tsirelson value with suitable measurements. Explicit permutation-invariant Dicke-state protocols violate CHSH above thresholds including 1/sqrt(2) for one excitation and the golden-ratio threshold asymptotically for larger excitation number.
main_result: The authors construct recovery-free CHSH protocols that tolerate particle loss above specific survival-probability thresholds.
application_angle: The results guide loss-tolerant designs for Bell tests, quantum repeaters, and photonic entanglement distribution.

title: Emergent non-Markovianity in time-delayed waveguide QED
abstract: Quantum systems are invariably coupled to a surrounding environment. A common theoretical method to simplify the problem is to trace over the environment under a Markov approximation, which assumes that the environment holds no memory over the timescales that the system evolves under. In interacting many-body systems, it is often not trivial to extract which of the multiple collective timescales are relevant. We consider a time-delayed waveguide QED setup with a single excitation. By fixing the maximum propagation time and increasing the number of emitters, we show that, even for small delay times, collective effects are sufficient to cause non-Markovianity. The impact of memory is intrinsically state-dependent. For superradiant states, the relevant system timescale is the superradiant lifetime while the relevant bath timescale is the end-to-end delay time. For subradiant states, both timescales depend on the structure of the specific state. Our results demonstrate the importance of prudently making Markov approximations in quantum many-body systems, and highlight potential pitfalls to avoid in scaling up quantum devices to large system sizes.
one_liner: Collective emitter dynamics can induce non-Markovian behavior in time-delayed waveguide QED even when delays are small.
why_it_matters: It warns that Markov approximations can fail as waveguide-QED devices scale, especially for collective superradiant and subradiant states.
detailed_summary: The study analyzes a single-excitation time-delayed waveguide-QED system while increasing emitter number at fixed maximum propagation time. It finds that collective many-body effects alone can generate non-Markovianity for small delays. The relevant system and bath timescales depend strongly on the state: superradiant states are governed by the superradiant lifetime and end-to-end delay, while subradiant states have state-structure-dependent timescales.
main_result: The main result is that scaling emitter number can make memory effects important even when individual propagation delays appear short.
application_angle: This matters for designing large photonic quantum devices where simplified Markovian models may mispredict performance.

title: Detuning-robust Rydberg entangling gates from echoed pulses
abstract: Rydberg-based two-qubit gate fidelities in neutral atom arrays are limited chiefly by laser intensity inhomogeneity and by detuning errors from frequency miscalibration, background-field drift, intermediate state light shift and Doppler shifts. Quantum optimal control can suppress the former, but no pulse can render a controlled-Z gate first-order insensitive to detuning. Here we show that this obstruction can be circumvented by designing Rydberg gate pulses with every leading-order detuning error relegated to single-qubit Z-rotations, which an echoed sequence removes. The resulting maximally-entangling ZZ gate has no leading-order response to arbitrary detunings on either atom, maintaining an infidelity below $10^{-3}$ much wider range of single-atom detunings than previous gate designs. We further show that a large fraction of residual error is dominated by population outside the computational subspace, which can be converted into heralded erasures. Our results significantly reduce the requirements on laser frequency stability and intensity homogeneity, field calibration and atomic temperature toward practical fault-tolerant quantum computing with neutral atoms.
one_liner: Echoed Rydberg pulse sequences convert leading detuning errors into removable single-qubit Z rotations for robust entangling gates.
why_it_matters: The method directly targets neutral-atom gate error sources such as detuning drift, Doppler shifts, and calibration imperfections.
detailed_summary: The paper shows that although no pulse can make a controlled-Z gate first-order insensitive to detuning, gate design can push leading detuning errors into single-qubit Z rotations. An echoed sequence cancels those rotations, yielding a maximally entangling ZZ gate with suppressed first-order response to arbitrary detunings on either atom. The design maintains sub-1e-3 infidelity over a broader detuning range than prior gates and identifies residual leakage that may be converted into heralded erasures.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a detuning-robust echoed Rydberg entangling gate with greatly reduced leading-order detuning sensitivity.
application_angle: This reduces stability and calibration demands for fault-tolerant neutral-atom quantum computing hardware.

title: Demystifying Relativistic Quantum Collapse
abstract: Non-relativistic objective collapse theories have been remarkably successful in addressing the conceptual problems of standard quantum mechanics. Despite substantial efforts, the project of extending them to the relativistic domain remains burdened by significant conceptual objections and technical challenges, often taken to cast doubt on the viability of the program as a whole. On the conceptual side, relativistic collapse theories have been claimed to face challenges involving tension between instantaneous collapse and relativity, frame-dependence of property values and probabilities, the possibility of superluminal signaling and the failure of narratability. On the technical side, persistent infinities, difficulties in constructing fully covariant frameworks and the apparent need for non-standard fields have hindered the development of workable models. In this paper, we offer a systematic rebuttal of the conceptual objections and provide a structured account of the remaining technical challenges. We conclude that relativistic collapse theories do provide a promising route toward a fully relativistic quantum framework that overcomes the conceptual limitations of standard quantum theory.
one_liner: A conceptual and technical defense of relativistic objective-collapse theories as viable relativistic quantum frameworks.
why_it_matters: While not an experimental sensing paper, it clarifies whether collapse models can remain compatible with relativity, signaling constraints, and covariant dynamics.
detailed_summary: The paper surveys standard objections to relativistic objective-collapse theories, including instantaneous collapse, frame-dependent properties, superluminal signaling, and narratability. It argues that these are not fatal conceptual barriers and separates them from remaining technical issues such as divergences, covariance, and non-standard fields. The result is a structured case that relativistic collapse remains a plausible route beyond standard quantum theory.
main_result: The work provides a systematic rebuttal of major conceptual objections and maps the technical obstacles that still need model-level solutions.
application_angle: Its relevance is indirect for sensing, but collapse models motivate precision tests of quantum mechanics and relativistic quantum behavior.

title: Real-Space Analysis of Two-Photon Polarization States in Type-II SPDC for High-Purity Polarization Entanglement
abstract: Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is one of the most widely used sources of polarization-entangled photon pairs, and understanding the generated biphoton state is essential for realizing high-brightness and high-purity entangled-photon sources. In particular, Type-II SPDC produces a biphoton wavefunction with a complex coupling between the spatial and polarization degrees of freedom owing to birefringence. In this study, we calculate the real-space distribution of the two-photon polarization state from the biphoton wavefunction of Type-II SPDC generated in a \b{eta}-barium borate (BBO) crystal. By identifying the spatial correlation direction between polarization and real-space coordinates, we designed aperture shapes that restrict the collection along this correlation direction. Through both numerical simulations and experiments, we demonstrate that such correlation-aligned apertures simultaneously achieve higher entanglement purity and improved photon collection efficiency. These results establish a practical design principle for optimizing aperture geometries based on the real-space biphoton wavefunction, providing a new approach to realizing high-purity and high-brightness SPDC entangled-photon sources.
one_liner: Real-space biphoton analysis guides aperture shapes that improve Type-II SPDC entanglement purity and collection efficiency.
why_it_matters: It gives a directly usable optical-design rule for brighter, cleaner polarization-entangled photon-pair sources.
detailed_summary: The authors compute the real-space distribution of the two-photon polarization state generated by Type-II SPDC in a BBO crystal, explicitly tracking spatial-polarization coupling from birefringence. They identify the direction along which real-space coordinates correlate with polarization and design collection apertures aligned to that correlation. Simulations and experiments show that these apertures raise both entanglement purity and photon collection efficiency.
main_result: Correlation-aligned apertures simultaneously improve polarization-entanglement purity and photon-pair collection efficiency.
application_angle: The approach is practical for high-brightness entangled-photon sources used in quantum communication, photonic experiments, and quantum networking.

title: Beyond geometric symmetry: Broadband linear relations in wave scattering
abstract: The design and control of wave scattering, that is, of the reflection and transmission parameters of a device, is of ubiquitous importance. These parameters generally change with varying frequency, though certain \emph{frequency-independent} linear relations may exist between them. Reciprocity and geometric symmetry (reflections, rotations, etc.) are classic and well-known examples that are present in many devices and significantly ease their design. In this work, we go beyond these and introduce a new class of relations that cannot be induced by reciprocity or geometric symmetry. Choosing networks of waveguides as our workhorse, we discuss the conditions and consequences of such novel behaviour and showcase suitable example setups. We further experimentally test our predictions using coaxial cables and find excellent agreement in the broad frequency range between 0 and 1 GHz. Our work not only deepens the theoretical understanding of waveguide network dynamics, but also opens new avenues for applications in broadband signal processing, quantum information, and integrated photonics.
one_liner: Broadband frequency-independent scattering relations are found beyond reciprocity or geometric symmetry and verified in coaxial networks.
why_it_matters: It expands the design toolkit for broadband wave devices, including integrated photonics and quantum-information signal routing.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces linear relations among reflection and transmission parameters that remain frequency independent but are not caused by reciprocity or standard geometric symmetries. Using waveguide-network models, it derives conditions under which these relations appear and studies their consequences for scattering control. Experiments with coaxial-cable networks confirm the predictions from 0 to 1 GHz with strong agreement.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a new class of broadband scattering constraints and experimentally validate them across 0-1 GHz.
application_angle: Such relations can simplify broadband component design for photonic circuits, RF signal processing, and quantum-information interconnects.

title: Auditing Structured Randomness for Quantum Error Correction under a Bounded Cloud Fault Model
abstract: Cloud quantum processors compile submitted quantum error correction circuits and may colocate them with untrusted workloads. A fixed public encoder gives a fault-injection adversary a reusable target. Per-run reseeding changes the physical-to-logical fault map. Exact Haar-random encoders have exponential circuit cost. Efficient random ensembles provide average-moment guarantees and leave worst-case accepted corruption uncharacterized. We define accepted logical disturbance, an acceptance-weighted measure of harmful logical action in accepted results, and derive its exact Haar expectation. We evaluate a polynomial-cost seeded Clifford encoder family using dense linear algebra and gate-level stabilizer simulation against faults chosen before or after the encoder is known. Reseeding reduces mean accepted logical disturbance from 0.150 for faults chosen after learning each encoder to 0.020 for one fault chosen before it is known. The 86.7% reduction results from rejection. The fixed distance-three \([[5,1,3]]\) code corrects every tested weight-one Pauli, while 18.5% of sampled encoders in the selected ensemble satisfy exact quantum error correction. The measured reduction quantifies the integrity gain from reseeding and separates postselected detection from exact correction under explicit fault and attacker-knowledge models.
one_liner: Seeded Clifford encoder reseeding reduces accepted logical disturbance in cloud QEC under explicit bounded fault attacks.
why_it_matters: It quantifies an integrity gain for cloud quantum processors where compiled QEC circuits may face adversarial or colocated fault injection.
detailed_summary: The paper defines accepted logical disturbance as an acceptance-weighted measure of harmful logical action that survives postselection. It compares Haar-random encoder expectations with a polynomial-cost seeded Clifford encoder family using dense linear algebra and gate-level stabilizer simulation. Under the studied bounded cloud fault model, reseeding reduces mean accepted logical disturbance from 0.150 to 0.020 when the fault must be chosen before the encoder is known.
main_result: Per-run encoder reseeding gives an 86.7% reduction in mean accepted logical disturbance through increased rejection of harmful faults.
application_angle: The technique is relevant to cloud quantum-computing integrity, especially where adversaries can exploit fixed public encoders.

title: Quantum estimation theory with quantum noise control
abstract: Quantum estimation theory serves as one of fundamental backbones of quantum Shannon information theory and was mathematically systematized by pioneers of quantum information science. Although its applied research saw limited progress for a long period, the 21st century has witnessed active discussions and numerous fruitful proposals regarding its applications. Notably, the contributions of Monras and Paris represent one of the most remarkable achievements addressing the realization problem of estimation bounds. This paper aims to demonstrate a practical direction for extending their original ideas. Next-generation quantum information mechanisms urgently demand guarantees of quantum advantage unattainable by classical theory, alongside strict real-time processing without delays. By leveraging the concept of generalized heterodyne detection proposed nearly half a century ago, we demonstrate that a scheme based on their results can effectively meet the stringent requirements of near-future information technologies.
one_liner: A quantum-estimation scheme using generalized heterodyne detection is proposed for real-time quantum noise control.
why_it_matters: It links estimation-bound theory to measurement architectures that could support low-latency quantum advantage claims in information systems.
detailed_summary: The paper revisits quantum estimation theory and the realization problem for estimation bounds, focusing on ideas associated with Monras and Paris. It proposes a practical extension based on generalized heterodyne detection as a route to quantum noise control. The claimed direction is aimed at systems needing both quantum-advantage guarantees and strict real-time operation.
main_result: The work argues that generalized heterodyne-based noise control can operationalize quantum-estimation bounds for real-time information processing.
application_angle: The framework is relevant to precision optical sensing and quantum receivers where estimator performance and measurement latency both matter.

title: A thermometric quantum Brownian model for low-temperature electronics
abstract: Quantum mechanical models of resistors in quantum electronics are often based on the quantum optical master equation (QOME). The QOME overlooks several fundamental properties, limiting its ability to model certain superconducting phenomena. Here we present a thermometric model of resistors, adapted from the quantum Brownian motion equation (QBME), that facilitates practical use of the QBME in modelling dissipative electronics at low temperatures. We compare the thermometric QBME presented here with predictions of the QOME, in the simple example of a transmon shunted by a resistor. We show that both the QBME and QOME yield comparable but physically distinct predictions, and discuss potential experimental tests with which to discriminate their use in modelling practical experiments.
one_liner: A thermometric quantum Brownian resistor model is developed for dissipative low-temperature quantum electronics.
why_it_matters: Accurate resistor modeling affects superconducting-circuit predictions, dissipation engineering, and interpretation of cryogenic experiments.
detailed_summary: The authors adapt the quantum Brownian motion equation into a thermometric resistor model for practical modeling of dissipative quantum electronics at low temperature. They compare this thermometric QBME approach with the commonly used quantum optical master equation in a transmon shunted by a resistor. The two models give comparable but physically distinct predictions, and the paper discusses experimental tests that could discriminate between them.
main_result: The paper provides a practical QBME-based resistor model and shows how its predictions differ from QOME-based modeling in a transmon example.
application_angle: This can improve modeling of cryogenic superconducting hardware where dissipation, thermalization, and resistor physics influence device behavior.

title: Observing relativistic trajectories of single photons
abstract: While the standard interpretation of quantum mechanics does not assign definite trajectories to particles, the Bohmian interpretation does. Only recently has an operational method for reconciling Bohmian mechanics with relativity been proposed. Here, we experimentally reconstruct relativistic Bohmian trajectories of a single photon in a Michelson-Sagnac interferometer, where counter-propagating probability amplitudes interfere head-on at the speed of light. As predicted by the relativistic Bohmian theory, we observe subluminal and superluminal features of the Bohmian trajectories of the photon traversing through the fringes. Our work provides experimental access to relativistic Bohmian mechanics and enables exploration of its unusual and counterintuitive properties.
one_liner: Single-photon relativistic Bohmian trajectories are reconstructed in a Michelson-Sagnac interferometer with head-on light-speed amplitudes.
why_it_matters: It gives an experimental handle on relativistic Bohmian dynamics in photonics, including trajectory features that can be subluminal or superluminal.
detailed_summary: The experiment uses a Michelson-Sagnac interferometer where counter-propagating single-photon probability amplitudes interfere head-on. From the optical interference data, the authors reconstruct relativistic Bohmian trajectories predicted by a recently proposed operational theory. The observed trajectories include subluminal and superluminal features as photons traverse the interference fringes, providing a photonic testbed for relativistic Bohmian mechanics.
main_result: The work experimentally reconstructs relativistic Bohmian trajectories of individual photons in an interferometric photonic system.
application_angle: The main practical value is a controllable optical platform for probing foundational trajectory models and relativistic quantum dynamics.

title: Measuring the Sr$^+$ 5s$_{1/2}$ Landé $g$-factor Using Singlet-Triplet Oscillations in a Circular Rydberg State of Strontium
abstract: Circular states of strontium are promising platforms for quantum technologies. They exhibit much longer lifetimes than laser-accessible Rydberg states and possess an optically active ionic core that can be manipulated with laser light. Here we trap circular states in optical tweezers by exploiting the dynamical polarizability of the ionic core. We measure the decay of the orbital component of a n=51 circular state and observe singlet-triplet spin oscillations arising from the interplay of vector light shifts induced by the optical tweezers, spin-orbit coupling associated with the Rydberg electron, and the difference in Landé $g$-factor between the ionic core and the Rydberg electrons. By observing the two electron spin dynamics, we measure the spin-orbit interaction and the correction $δg \sim$ 10^(-5) of the Landé $g$-factor of the Sr$^+$ 5s$_{1/2}$ ionic core electron with respect to that of a free electron. This provides a first high-precision measurement of $g_{\textrm{Sr}^+, 5s_{1/2}}$ = 2.002290(1).
one_liner: Circular Rydberg strontium states in optical tweezers are used to measure the Sr+ 5s1/2 Landé g-factor at high precision.
why_it_matters: Circular Rydberg alkaline-earth atoms combine long-lived states with an optically active core, making them promising for quantum hardware and precision control.
detailed_summary: The authors trap n=51 circular Rydberg states of strontium in optical tweezers by exploiting the ionic core's dynamical polarizability. They observe singlet-triplet spin oscillations driven by vector light shifts, Rydberg spin-orbit coupling, and the small g-factor difference between the ionic core and Rydberg electrons. Analysis of the two-electron spin dynamics yields the spin-orbit interaction and a correction of order 1e-5 to the Sr+ 5s1/2 core electron Landé factor.
platform_or_system: optically trapped circular Rydberg strontium atoms
main_result: The paper reports g(Sr+ 5s1/2) = 2.002290(1) from singlet-triplet oscillations in trapped circular Rydberg strontium.
application_angle: The result supports precision calibration and coherent control of circular Rydberg platforms for neutral-atom quantum technologies.

title: Split Coaxial Cable Medium for Tunable Artificial Dielectrics and Plasmas
abstract: We introduce the Split Coaxial Cable Medium (SCCM), a mechanically tunable, capacitively loaded wire medium supporting artificial-dielectric and artificial-plasma Bloch regimes with high in-plane isotropy. Its unit cell comprises coaxial conductors interrupted by axial gaps. Relative axial displacement continuously varies their capacitive overlap and series capacitance while preserving the transverse lattice geometry and leaving the unit-cell inductance approximately unchanged. Equivalent RLC parameters are derived directly from the geometry and incorporated into complementary analytical models. A spatially dispersive local-field model predicts the Bloch dispersion and isofrequency contours, whereas a multilayer homogenization model provides the modal impedance, closed-form estimates of the low-frequency Bloch refractive index and plasma frequency, and loss-inclusive finite-slab scattering. Full-wave eigenmode and finite-slab simulations validate the predictions. Over the investigated displacement range, simulations yield tunabilities of $46\%$ in the low-frequency Bloch refractive index, from $n_{0,\min}=1.42$ to $n_{0,\max}=2.28$, and $21\%$ in the plasma frequency, from $f_{\mathrm{p},\min}=9.45~\mathrm{GHz}$ to $f_{\mathrm{p},\max}=11.61~\mathrm{GHz}$, while confirming high in-plane isotropy near the $Γ$ point in both regimes. These characteristics make the SCCM promising for gradient-index devices, directive antennas, and tunable plasma haloscopes.
one_liner: A split coaxial cable medium enables mechanically tunable artificial dielectric and plasma behavior in microwave metamaterials.
why_it_matters: The design offers large refractive-index and plasma-frequency tuning while preserving in-plane isotropy, useful for reconfigurable photonic and RF devices.
detailed_summary: The Split Coaxial Cable Medium uses coaxial conductors interrupted by axial gaps, where relative displacement tunes capacitive overlap and series capacitance while largely preserving inductance and lattice geometry. Analytical RLC, local-field, and homogenization models are developed for Bloch dispersion, impedance, refractive index, plasma frequency, and finite-slab scattering. Full-wave simulations validate the models and show 46% tunability in low-frequency Bloch refractive index and 21% tunability in plasma frequency with high in-plane isotropy near the Gamma point.
main_result: Simulations show refractive-index tuning from 1.42 to 2.28 and plasma-frequency tuning from 9.45 GHz to 11.61 GHz.
application_angle: The platform is relevant to tunable gradient-index components, directive antennas, and plasma-haloscopes for sensing applications.

title: Bound-state-mediated remote charging of a quantum battery
abstract: Remote charging of a quantum battery (QB) is hindered by radiative leakage of the excitation into the photonic environment that acts as a mediator for energy transfer. We consider a charger-battery model consisting of two two-level systems (TLSs) that are locally coupled to two sites of a one-dimensional coupled cavity array. When their transition frequency lies outside the propagation band, the system forms atom-photon bound states with localized photonic components, and the overlap of these components lifts the degeneracy of the even- and odd-parity bound states, yielding an energy splitting that drives coherent energy transfer from the charger to the QB. In this way, the band gap suppresses resonant emission and the localized bound states mediate remote charging. From the parity-resolved spectrum, we relate the charging time to the energy splitting and the charged ergotropy to the fraction of TLS population on the bound states. Bound states closer to the band edge extend the interaction range of the TLSs but contain a large photonic fraction and are consequently more susceptible to photon loss.
one_liner: Atom-photon bound states in a coupled-cavity array mediate coherent remote charging between two two-level systems.
why_it_matters: It identifies a route to suppress radiative leakage while transferring energy remotely, a key issue for distributed quantum batteries.
detailed_summary: The model contains charger and battery two-level systems locally coupled to separated sites of a one-dimensional coupled-cavity array. When the transition frequency is outside the propagation band, atom-photon bound states form with localized photonic components whose overlap splits even- and odd-parity states. This splitting drives coherent remote energy transfer, while the band gap suppresses resonant emission; the analysis links charging time to the splitting and ergotropy to bound-state TLS population.
platform_or_system: two-level systems coupled to a 1D cavity array
main_result: The paper shows that localized bound states can mediate remote quantum-battery charging while reducing radiative loss.
application_angle: The mechanism is relevant for photonic quantum hardware where energy transfer must occur over distance without excessive leakage.

title: Quantum Interconnects Part I: Strategic Quantum Network Formation
abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum networks requires more than advances in quantum repeaters, memories, and processors, it requires a framework explaining how heterogeneous quantum technologies evolve from isolated deployments into interconnected infrastructures. While the classical Internet evolved under strong utility incentives associated with resource sharing and communication demands, quantum networking currently lacks dominant applications capable of generating comparable incentives. As a consequence, contemporary quantum networks are largely formed through technology-driven decisions motivated by technical feasibility, experimental validation, and expected future value. This work argues that the absence of utility-driven network formation is not solely a consequence of immature applications, but also of insufficient abstraction. In particular, heterogeneous quantum platforms remain tightly coupled to the functionalities they provide, preventing the definition of technology-independent utility functions. A hierarchical architecture consisting of Physical Platforms (PP), Functionalities (F), Services (S), Applications (A), and Use-Cases (UC) is proposed, together with the argument that quantum interconnects constitute the enabling technology required to decouple physical implementations from network functionalities. Such decoupling permits the definition of utility functions at the functionality level and establishes the conditions under which strategic (agent-based) network formation becomes applicable. Quantum interconnects should therefore be viewed not only as interoperability devices, but also as fundamental enablers of strategic quantum network evolution.
one_liner: A layered architecture is proposed to explain how quantum interconnects can enable strategic formation of heterogeneous quantum networks.
why_it_matters: It reframes interconnects as infrastructure that decouples physical platforms from services, helping quantum networks evolve beyond isolated demonstrations.
detailed_summary: The paper argues that quantum-network deployment is currently driven more by technical feasibility and expected future value than by immediate utility incentives. It proposes a hierarchy of Physical Platforms, Functionalities, Services, Applications, and Use-Cases to separate implementation details from network-level value. Quantum interconnects are positioned as the enabling layer that decouples heterogeneous hardware from functionality, making agent-based strategic network formation applicable.
main_result: The work presents a conceptual architecture in which quantum interconnects enable utility-driven strategic quantum network evolution.
application_angle: The framework is relevant for planning interoperable quantum-network infrastructure and identifying where interconnect technology creates deployable value.

title: Correcting Connectivity in Arc-Based QUBO Models for Fixed-Fleet Vehicle Routing
abstract: We revisit a degree-only arc Hamiltonian for fixed-fleet, homogeneous, uncapacitated vehicle routing. Because its local penalties define only a cycle cover, ground states may contain customer cycles disconnected from the depot. We construct a polynomial-size quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) repair using capped single-commodity flow and prove that every ground-state routing is connected and cost-optimal under explicit penalty assumptions. For $N-1$ customers and $K$ nonempty routes, the unreduced encoding uses exactly $|E|(1+\lceil\log_2(N-K+1)\rceil)$ logical problem qubits. A reversible compute--phase--uncompute realization evaluates the flow penalties in $O(N^2\log N+N\log^2N)$ logical gates on a complete graph with $O(\log N)$ reusable workspace and no product register. On complete loopless graphs, a depot-delimited single-sequence position encoding uses fewer problem qubits and fewer written terms when the flow-word length grows. Conversely, the flow model achieves a smaller structured logical-gate upper bound under a common reversible accounting model. Exact audits of the Hamiltonian and circuit implementation, combined with a $1{,}200$-matrix classical benchmark, verify the formulation and quantify the connectivity gap. Finally, a 32,000-shot Amazon Braket task on IQM Emerald characterizes depth-one termwise Ising circuits on a diagnostic $N = 4,\, K = 1$ counterexample instance. In the degree-only circuit, $78.05\%$ of selected $p=1$ shots realize the invalid disconnected ground state; the reduced 14-qubit flow-augmented circuit yields no fully feasible sample. These device results characterize mapped Hamiltonians and compilation rather than an asymptotic routing solution advantage.
one_liner: A flow-augmented QUBO repair fixes disconnected-cycle failures in fixed-fleet vehicle-routing Hamiltonians and is tested on IQM hardware.
